h: Norman roots and a clever design
p: The story of the castle here goes right back to William the Conqueror, who built a wooden castle on this spot in 1068 to keep a grip on the north. The stone tower you see today was built in the thirteenth century under Henry III, and its unusual four-lobed shape, a bit like a clover leaf, makes it unlike almost any other castle in England. Look at it from the bottom of the mound and you'll see what we mean.

The name is thought to come from Roger de Clifford, a rebel executed in 1322 whose body was reportedly hung in chains from the tower. It's a grim tale, but older kids love a gory detail. English Heritage reopened the tower in 2022 after a big project that added walkways inside and the rooftop deck, so you can now see more of the inside of the walls than before.

Make a morning of it in this part of town. Jorvik Viking Centre on Coppergate is a short walk away and brings Viking-age York to life, sounds and smells included. Fairfax House, a beautiful Georgian townhouse on Castlegate, is also right on the doorstep for anyone who likes elegant interiors.
With so much packed into this corner of the city, you can easily cover the tower, a museum and lunch without walking far.
